29  Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Equations

An ordinary differential equation specifies the instantaneous velocity of a continuous state trajectory. A numerical time-stepping method replaces this continuous flow by a sequence of computable discrete states. The core mathematical questions in numerical ODE integration are consistency, zero-stability, global convergence, stiffness, and geometric structure preservation.

29.1 Initial Value Problems and Well-Posedness

NoteDefinition: Initial Value Problem

An initial value problem (IVP) for a system of ordinary differential equations has the form \[ \begin{align} \by'(t) = \boldsymbol{f}(t, \by(t)), \qquad \by(t_0) = \by_0, \end{align} \] where \(t \in [t_0, T]\) and \(\by(t) \in \fR^m\). The function \(\boldsymbol{f}: [t_0, T] \times \fR^m \to \fR^m\) is the vector field.

NoteTheorem: Picard–Lindelöf Existence and Uniqueness

Let \(\boldsymbol{f}(t, \by)\) be continuous in \(t\) and uniformly Lipschitz continuous in \(\by\) on the domain \([t_0, T] \times \fR^m\): \[ \begin{align} \|\boldsymbol{f}(t, \bu) - \boldsymbol{f}(t, \bv)\| \leq L \|\bu - \bv\| \qquad \text{for all } \bu, \bv \in \fR^m, \end{align} \] where \(L < \infty\) is the Lipschitz constant. Then the IVP has a unique continuous solution \(\by(t)\) on \([t_0, T]\).

TipProof

The differential equation \(\by' = \boldsymbol{f}(t, \by)\) with initial condition \(\by(t_0) = \by_0\) is equivalent to the Picard integral equation: \[ \begin{align} \by(t) = \by_0 + \int_{t_0}^t \boldsymbol{f}(s, \by(s))\,ds. \end{align} \] Assume first that \(L>0\). Define the Picard operator \(\mathcal{T}\) on the Banach space \(C([t_0, T]; \fR^m)\) equipped with the weighted norm \(\|\by\|_* = \max_{t \in [t_0, T]} e^{-2L(t-t_0)} \|\by(t)\|\). For any two functions \(\bu, \bv\): \[ \begin{align} \|(\mathcal{T}\bu)(t) - (\mathcal{T}\bv)(t)\| &\leq \int_{t_0}^t \|\boldsymbol{f}(s, \bu(s)) - \boldsymbol{f}(s, \bv(s))\|\,ds \\ &\leq L \int_{t_0}^t \|\bu(s) - \bv(s)\|\,ds \\ &= L \int_{t_0}^t e^{2L(s-t_0)} \left( e^{-2L(s-t_0)} \|\bu(s) - \bv(s)\| \right) ds \\ &\leq L \|\bu - \bv\|_* \int_{t_0}^t e^{2L(s-t_0)}\,ds \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \left(e^{2L(t-t_0)}-1\right)\|\bu-\bv\|_*. \end{align} \] Multiplying through by \(e^{-2L(t-t_0)}\) yields \(\|\mathcal{T}\bu - \mathcal{T}\bv\|_* \leq \frac{1}{2} \|\bu - \bv\|_*\). Because the operator \(\mathcal{T}\) is a strict contraction with modulus \(1/2\) on a complete metric space, the Banach Fixed-Point Theorem guarantees the existence of a unique fixed point \(\by^* = \mathcal{T}\by^*\), which is the unique solution to the IVP. If \(L=0\), then \(\boldsymbol f(t,\bu)=\boldsymbol f(t,\bv)\) for every \(\bu,\bv\), so \(\mathcal{T}\) has contraction modulus zero in the ordinary supremum norm.

29.2 Consistency, Stability, and the Discrete Gronwall Lemma

A numerical time-stepping method is convergent if the computed trajectory approaches the exact trajectory as the step size \(h \to 0\). We quantify error at each step and track its accumulation over a finite time interval.

NoteDefinition: Local Truncation Error and One-Step Defect

Let \(\by_{n+1} = \Phi_h(t_n, \by_n)\) denote an autonomous or non-autonomous one-step method. The local truncation error is the defect of the exact solution: \[ \begin{align} \boldsymbol{\tau}_{n+1} = \frac{\by(t_{n+1}) - \Phi_h(t_n, \by(t_n))}{h}. \end{align} \] The method is consistent of order \(p\) if \(\|\boldsymbol{\tau}_{n+1}\| = O(h^p)\) as \(h \to 0\) for all sufficiently smooth solutions.

NoteLemma: Discrete Gronwall Lemma

Let \(\{e_n\}_{n=0}^N\) be a sequence of non-negative real numbers satisfying the linear recurrence \[ \begin{align} e_{n+1} \leq (1 + \alpha) e_n + \beta, \qquad n = 0, 1, ..., N-1, \end{align} \] where \(\alpha, \beta \geq 0\). For \(\alpha>0\), \[ \begin{align} e_n \leq e^{n \alpha} e_0 + \beta \frac{e^{n \alpha} - 1}{\alpha}. \end{align} \] For \(\alpha=0\), the corresponding bound is \(e_n\leq e_0+n\beta\).

TipProof

Expanding the recurrence by induction gives \[ \begin{align} e_n \leq (1 + \alpha)^n e_0 + \beta \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (1 + \alpha)^k = (1 + \alpha)^n e_0 + \beta \frac{(1 + \alpha)^n - 1}{\alpha}. \end{align} \] Using the standard inequality \(1 + \alpha \leq e^\alpha\) for all \(\alpha \geq 0\), we have \((1 + \alpha)^n \leq (e^\alpha)^n = e^{n \alpha}\), which completes the proof.

NoteTheorem: Fundamental Theorem of One-Step Convergence

Let \(\Phi_h\) be a consistent one-step method of order \(p\) applied to an IVP whose vector field \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is Lipschitz continuous with constant \(L\). Suppose the numerical increment function satisfies \(\|\Phi_h(t, \bu) - \Phi_h(t, \bv)\| \leq (1 + \Lambda h) \|\bu - \bv\|\) for some constant \(\Lambda \geq 0\). Then on the fixed interval \([t_0, T]\) with \(Nh = T - t_0\), the global error \(\be_n = \by(t_n) - \by_n\) satisfies \[ \begin{align} \max_{0 \leq n \leq N} \|\be_n\| \leq e^{\Lambda(T - t_0)} \|\be_0\| + \frac{e^{\Lambda(T - t_0)} - 1}{\Lambda} \max_k \|\boldsymbol{\tau}_k\|, \end{align} \] where the quotient is interpreted as \(T-t_0\) when \(\Lambda=0\). Consequently, when the numerical and exact solutions use the same initial value, a local error of order \(O(h^{p+1})\) yields a global error of order \(O(h^p)\).

TipProof

Express the error at step \(n+1\) by subtracting the numerical update from the exact solution: \[ \begin{align} \be_{n+1} &= \by(t_{n+1}) - \by_{n+1} \\ &= \left[ \Phi_h(t_n, \by(t_n)) + h \boldsymbol{\tau}_{n+1} \right] - \Phi_h(t_n, \by_n) \\ &= \left[ \Phi_h(t_n, \by(t_n)) - \Phi_h(t_n, \by_n) \right] + h \boldsymbol{\tau}_{n+1}. \end{align} \] Taking norms and applying the triangle inequality yields \[ \begin{align} \|\be_{n+1}\| \leq (1 + \Lambda h) \|\be_n\| + h \max_k \|\boldsymbol{\tau}_k\|. \end{align} \] Applying the Discrete Gronwall Lemma (the result above) with \(\alpha = \Lambda h\) and \(\beta = h \max_k \|\boldsymbol{\tau}_k\|\) gives \[ \begin{align} \|\be_n\| \leq e^{n \Lambda h} \|\be_0\| + h \max_k \|\boldsymbol{\tau}_k\| \frac{e^{n \Lambda h} - 1}{\Lambda h} = e^{\Lambda(t_n - t_0)} \|\be_0\| + \frac{e^{\Lambda(t_n - t_0)} - 1}{\Lambda} \max_k \|\boldsymbol{\tau}_k\|. \end{align} \] Since \(t_n - t_0 \leq T - t_0\) and \(\max_k \|\boldsymbol{\tau}_k\| = O(h^p)\), the global error is bounded by \(O(h^p)\) when initial data are exact (\(\be_0 = \bzero\)).

29.3 Euler Methods and Stability Functions

NoteDefinition: Forward Euler, Backward Euler, and Trapezoidal Methods

For time step \(h = t_{n+1} - t_n\):

  1. Forward Euler (explicit): \(\by_{n+1} = \by_n + h \boldsymbol{f}(t_n, \by_n)\).

  2. Backward Euler (implicit): \(\by_{n+1} = \by_n + h \boldsymbol{f}(t_{n+1}, \by_{n+1})\).

  3. Trapezoidal Rule (implicit Crank–Nicolson): \[ \begin{align} \by_{n+1} = \by_n + \frac{h}{2} \left[ \boldsymbol{f}(t_n, \by_n) + \boldsymbol{f}(t_{n+1}, \by_{n+1}) \right]. \end{align} \]

NoteTheorem: Stability Functions for Linear Test Equations

Applied to the Dahlquist test equation \(y' = \lambda y\) with \(z = h\lambda \in \fC\), the numerical update satisfies \(y_{n+1} = R(z) y_n\). The stability functions are: \[ \begin{align} R_{\mathrm{FE}}(z) = 1 + z, \qquad R_{\mathrm{BE}}(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z}, \qquad R_{\mathrm{TR}}(z) = \frac{1 + z/2}{1 - z/2}. \end{align} \] The region of absolute stability is \(\mathcal{S} = \{z \in \fC : |R(z)| \leq 1\}\). Backward Euler and the Trapezoidal Rule are A-stable: \(\fC^- = \{z \in \fC : \operatorname{Re}(z) \leq 0\} \subseteq \mathcal{S}\). Backward Euler is additionally L-stable: \(\lim_{z \to -\infty} R_{\mathrm{BE}}(z) = 0\).

TipProof

For Forward Euler: \(y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_n = (1 + z)y_n\). For Backward Euler: \(y_{n+1} = y_n + z y_{n+1} \implies (1 - z)y_{n+1} = y_n \implies y_{n+1} = \frac{1}{1 - z} y_n\). For Trapezoidal Rule: \(y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{z}{2}(y_n + y_{n+1}) \implies (1 - z/2)y_{n+1} = (1 + z/2)y_n \implies y_{n+1} = \frac{1 + z/2}{1 - z/2} y_n\). Let \(z = x + iy\) with \(x \leq 0\). For Backward Euler, \(|1 - z|^2 = (1 - x)^2 + y^2 \geq 1 + y^2 \geq 1\), so \(|R_{\mathrm{BE}}(z)| = \frac{1}{|1 - z|} \leq 1\). For Trapezoidal Rule, \[ \begin{align} |1 + z/2|^2 = (1 + x/2)^2 + (y/2)^2 = 1 + x + \frac{x^2 + y^2}{4}, \\ |1 - z/2|^2 = (1 - x/2)^2 + (y/2)^2 = 1 - x + \frac{x^2 + y^2}{4}. \end{align} \] Because \(x \leq 0\), we have \(1 + x \leq 1 - x\), which implies \(|1 + z/2|^2 \leq |1 - z/2|^2\) and \(|R_{\mathrm{TR}}(z)| \leq 1\). Thus both methods are A-stable. Along the negative real axis, \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} |R_{\mathrm{BE}}(x)| = \lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac{1}{1 - x} = 0\), proving L-stability. In contrast, \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} R_{\mathrm{TR}}(x) = -1\), so the Trapezoidal Rule is not L-stable.

29.4 Runge–Kutta Methods

Runge–Kutta methods achieve high orders of accuracy without storing historical steps by evaluating intermediate stages within each time step.

NoteDefinition: Classical Fourth-Order Runge–Kutta Method (RK4)

For an autonomous ODE \(\by' = \boldsymbol{f}(\by)\), the classical RK4 method computes four stages: \[ \begin{align} \boldsymbol{k}_1 &= \boldsymbol{f}(\by_n), \\ \boldsymbol{k}_2 &= \boldsymbol{f}\left( \by_n + \frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{k}_1 \right), \\ \boldsymbol{k}_3 &= \boldsymbol{f}\left( \by_n + \frac{h}{2}\boldsymbol{k}_2 \right), \\ \boldsymbol{k}_4 &= \boldsymbol{f}\left( \by_n + h\boldsymbol{k}_3 \right), \end{align} \] and sets the update \[ \begin{align} \by_{n+1} = \by_n + \frac{h}{6} \left( \boldsymbol{k}_1 + 2\boldsymbol{k}_2 + 2\boldsymbol{k}_3 + \boldsymbol{k}_4 \right). \end{align} \] The one-step defect is \(O(h^5)\). With the normalization in the result above, the local truncation error and the global error are both \(O(h^4)\).

NoteTheorem: RK4 Stability Polynomial

Applied to the scalar linear test equation \(y' = \lambda y\), the stability function of RK4 is \[ \begin{align} R(z) = 1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{6} + \frac{z^4}{24} = \sum_{k=0}^4 \frac{z^k}{k!}, \qquad z = h\lambda. \end{align} \]

TipProof

Substituting \(f(y) = \lambda y\) into the RK4 stages: \[ \begin{align} k_1 &= \lambda y_n, \\ k_2 &= \lambda \left( y_n + \frac{h}{2} k_1 \right) = \lambda \left( 1 + \frac{z}{2} \right) y_n, \\ k_3 &= \lambda \left( y_n + \frac{h}{2} k_2 \right) = \lambda \left( 1 + \frac{z}{2} + \frac{z^2}{4} \right) y_n, \\ k_4 &= \lambda \left( y_n + h k_3 \right) = \lambda \left( 1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{4} \right) y_n. \end{align} \] Substituting these into the update formula: \[ \begin{align} y_{n+1} &= y_n + \frac{h}{6} \left[ \lambda + 2\lambda\left(1 + \frac{z}{2}\right) + 2\lambda\left(1 + \frac{z}{2} + \frac{z^2}{4}\right) + \lambda\left(1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{4}\right) \right] y_n \\ &= y_n + \frac{z}{6} \left[ 1 + (2 + z) + \left(2 + z + \frac{z^2}{2}\right) + \left(1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{4}\right) \right] y_n \\ &= y_n + \frac{z}{6} \left[ 6 + 3z + z^2 + \frac{z^3}{4} \right] y_n \\ &= \left( 1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{6} + \frac{z^4}{24} \right) y_n. \end{align} \]

29.5 Symplectic Integrators and Geometric Mechanics

Hamiltonian systems preserve geometric phase-space volume and energy. Standard Runge–Kutta methods dissipate or amplify energy over long integration horizons. Symplectic integrators preserve the underlying canonical symplectic 2-form.

NoteDefinition: Velocity Verlet Algorithm

For a separable Hamiltonian \(H(\bq, \bv) = \frac{1}{2}\|\bv\|_2^2 + V(\bq)\) with equations of motion \(\bq' = \bv\) and \(\bv' = \bF(\bq) = -\nabla V(\bq)\), the Velocity Verlet method is: \[ \begin{align} \bv_{n+1/2} &= \bv_n + \frac{h}{2} \bF(\bq_n), \\ \bq_{n+1} &= \bq_n + h \bv_{n+1/2}, \\ \bv_{n+1} &= \bv_{n+1/2} + \frac{h}{2} \bF(\bq_{n+1}). \end{align} \]

NoteTheorem: Symplecticity and Area Preservation of Velocity Verlet

The one-step Velocity Verlet map \(\Psi_h: (\bq_n, \bv_n) \mapsto (\bq_{n+1}, \bv_{n+1})\) preserves the canonical symplectic structure. In particular, the Jacobian matrix \(\bJ = \frac{\partial(\bq_{n+1}, \bv_{n+1})}{\partial(\bq_n, \bv_n)}\) satisfies \[ \begin{align} \det(\bJ) = 1. \end{align} \] Equivalently, its Jacobian satisfies \(\bJ^T\boldsymbol{\Omega}\bJ=\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) for the canonical symplectic matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\). Symplecticity implies \(\det(\bJ)=1\), so Velocity Verlet also preserves phase-space volume.

TipProof

Decompose the Velocity Verlet step into the composition of three elementary shears: \[ \begin{align} \Psi_h = \psi_3 \circ \psi_2 \circ \psi_1, \end{align} \] where: \[ \begin{align} \psi_1(\bq, \bv) &= \left( \bq,\, \bv + \frac{h}{2}\bF(\bq) \right), \\ \psi_2(\bq, \bv) &= (\bq + h\bv,\, \bv), \\ \psi_3(\bq, \bv) &= \left( \bq,\, \bv + \frac{h}{2}\bF(\bq) \right). \end{align} \] Evaluating the Jacobian of each shear map: \[ \begin{align} \bJ_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ \frac{h}{2}\nabla\bF(\bq) & \bI \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \bJ_2 = \begin{pmatrix} \bI & h\bI \\ \bzero & \bI \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \bJ_3 = \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ \frac{h}{2}\nabla\bF(\bq_{n+1}) & \bI \end{pmatrix}. \end{align} \] Because \(\bF=-\nabla V\), the Hessian block \(\bS = \frac{h}{2}\nabla\bF = -\frac{h}{2}\nabla^2V\) is symmetric (\(\bS^T = \bS\)). With canonical symplectic matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Omega} = \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix}\), evaluating the quadratic form for \(\bJ_1\): \[ \begin{align} \bJ_1^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_1 &= \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bS \\ \bzero & \bI \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ \bS & \bI \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} -\bS & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ \bS & \bI \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\bS + \bS & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix} = \boldsymbol{\Omega}. \end{align} \] Similarly, for the translation shear \(\bJ_2\): \[ \begin{align} \bJ_2^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_2 &= \begin{pmatrix} \bI & \bzero \\ h\bI & \bI \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & \bzero \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bI & h\bI \\ \bzero & \bI \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & h\bI \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \bI & h\bI \\ \bzero & \bI \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \bzero & \bI \\ -\bI & -h\bI + h\bI \end{pmatrix} = \boldsymbol{\Omega}. \end{align} \] The third shear \(\bJ_3\) has the same form as \(\bJ_1\) and satisfies \(\bJ_3^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_3 = \boldsymbol{\Omega}\). By the chain rule, \(\bJ = \bJ_3 \bJ_2 \bJ_1\), so \[ \begin{align} \bJ^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ = \bJ_1^T \bJ_2^T \left( \bJ_3^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_3 \right) \bJ_2 \bJ_1 = \bJ_1^T \left( \bJ_2^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_2 \right) \bJ_1 = \bJ_1^T \boldsymbol{\Omega} \bJ_1 = \boldsymbol{\Omega}. \end{align} \] Each shear has unit determinant: \(\det(\bJ_1) = \det(\bJ_2) = \det(\bJ_3) = 1\). Therefore \[ \begin{align} \det(\bJ) = \det(\bJ_3)\det(\bJ_2)\det(\bJ_1) = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1. \end{align} \]

29.6 Exercises

WarningExercise

  1. Derive. The discrete Gronwall lemma and Forward Euler convergence.

    1. Let \(\by(t)\) solve \(\by' = \boldsymbol{f}(t, \by)\) with \(\|\boldsymbol{f}(t, \bu) - \boldsymbol{f}(t, \bv)\| \leq L\|\bu - \bv\|\). Use Taylor’s theorem to show that the one-step defect of Forward Euler satisfies \(\|\by(t_{n+1}) - (\by(t_n) + h\boldsymbol{f}(t_n, \by(t_n)))\| \leq \frac{h^2}{2} M_2\), where \(M_2 = \max \|\by''(t)\|\).

    2. Derive the error recurrence \(\|\be_{n+1}\| \leq (1 + Lh)\|\be_n\| + \frac{h^2}{2}M_2\).

    3. Apply the result above to establish the rigorous global error bound \(\|\be_n\| \leq \frac{M_2}{2L}(e^{L(t_n - t_0)} - 1)h\).

  2. Derive. A-stability and L-stability of implicit methods.

    1. Plot the boundary of the Forward Euler stability region \(|1 + z| = 1\) in the complex plane. Show that for real \(\lambda < 0\), stability requires \(h \leq 2/|\lambda|\).

    2. For the implicit Trapezoidal Rule, prove that \(|R_{\mathrm{TR}}(z)| = 1\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Re}(z) = 0\). Explain why this implies that undamped physical oscillations are integrated without artificial numerical dissipation.

    3. Apply the Trapezoidal Rule and Backward Euler to the stiff problem \(y' = -1000y\), \(y(0) = 1\) with \(h = 0.1\). Show that Trapezoidal Rule produces oscillatory values \((-99/101)^n \approx (-0.98)^n\), whereas Backward Euler dampens the mode immediately to \((1/101)^n \approx 10^{-2n}\).

  3. Explore. Symplectic geometry of the harmonic oscillator. Consider the harmonic oscillator \(q' = v\), \(v' = -q\) with exact energy \(E(q, v) = \frac{1}{2}(q^2 + v^2)\).

    1. Compute the one-step update matrix \(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{FE}}\) for Forward Euler and show that \(\det(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{FE}}) = 1 + h^2 > 1\).

    2. Compute the one-step update matrix \(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Verlet}}\) for Velocity Verlet. Confirm that \(\det(\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Verlet}}) = 1\).

    3. Show that Velocity Verlet conserves an exact modified shadow Hamiltonian \(\tilde{H}(q, v) = \frac{1}{2}(q^2 + v^2) - \frac{h^2}{4}q^2 = H(q, v) + O(h^2)\).

  4. Compute. Adaptive step size control via embedded Runge–Kutta pairs.

    1. An embedded pair computes a lower-order approximation \(\by_{n+1}^{[p]}\) and a higher-order approximation \(\by_{n+1}^{[p+1]}\) sharing stages. Show that the difference \(\be_{n+1} = \by_{n+1}^{[p+1]} - \by_{n+1}^{[p]}\) satisfies \(\|\be_{n+1}\| = C h^{p+1} + O(h^{p+2})\).

    2. Given error tolerance \(\varepsilon\) and current step size \(h_{\mathrm{old}}\), derive the optimal step size formula \(h_{\mathrm{new}} = s h_{\mathrm{old}} (\varepsilon / \|\be_{n+1}\|)^{1/(p+1)}\) with safety factor \(s \in (0, 1)\).

    3. Explain why adaptive solvers reject a step and repeat with smaller \(h\) when \(\|\be_{n+1}\| > \varepsilon\), and why step growth is capped by \(h_{\mathrm{new}} \leq 5 h_{\mathrm{old}}\) in production codes.

  5. Explore. Stiffness in chemical cascades and BDF methods. Consider the singularly perturbed initial value problem \(\varepsilon y' = -y + \cos(t)\) with \(y(0) = 0\) and \(\varepsilon = 10^{-4}\).

    1. Find the exact solution and identify the fast boundary layer transient \(e^{-t/\varepsilon}\) and the slow quasi-steady state \(\cos(t) + \varepsilon \sin(t)\).

    2. Explain why explicit RK4 requires \(h \lesssim 2.8 \times 10^{-4}\) throughout the entire simulation, even after the transient has decayed to zero.

    3. Formulate the BDF2 update \(\frac{3\by_{n+1} - 4\by_n + \by_{n-1}}{2h} = \boldsymbol{f}(t_{n+1}, \by_{n+1})\) and show that it allows time steps \(h = 0.1\) in the smooth regime.

NoteFurther reading

Hairer, N{}rsett, and Wanner give a careful account of ODE methods and their analysis (Hairer et al. 1993). Dahlquist’s paper is the classical source for the stability barrier for linear multistep methods (Dahlquist 1963). Quarteroni, Sacco, and Saleri provide a broader numerical-analysis reference (Quarteroni et al. 2007).

Dahlquist, Germund G. 1963. “A Special Stability Problem for Linear Multistep Methods.” BIT Numerical Mathematics 3: 27–43. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01963532.
Hairer, Ernst, Syvert P. Nørsett, and Gerhard Wanner. 1993. Solving Ordinary Differential Equations i: Nonstiff Problems. 2nd ed. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-78862-1.
Quarteroni, Alfio, Riccardo Sacco, and Fausto Saleri. 2007. Numerical Mathematics. 2nd ed. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/b98885.
